phrases.japanese: 倉庫に他にもありますか？
phrases.romaji: Sōko ni hoka ni mo arimasu ka?
phrases.meaning: Do you have more in the stockroom?
phrases.usageNote: Use at Hard Off when floor stock looks thin or condition-graded poorly — staff sometimes have better pieces not yet shelved. Works best if you point at the category section.

phrases.romaji: Moto no hako wa arimasu ka?
phrases.meaning: Does this come with the original box?
phrases.usageNote: Complete-in-box adds significant resale value, especially for retro gaming and electronics. Always ask before committing — the box may be stored separately at the counter.

phrases.japanese: 付属品は揃っていますか？
phrases.usageNote: Chargers, straps, and original manuals affect resale price. A watch without its original bracelet or strap can sell for 20–40% less to Western collectors.

phrases.meaning: Is this the only one you have?
phrases.usageNote: Direct follow-up when the only piece is low-grade or overpriced. Sometimes prompts staff to mention a similar item in a different section you haven't spotted yet.
Forces transparency. JP shops grade conservatively, so a stated B-grade often has only minor marks. Ask before buying anything above ¥5,000 — staff will point out every flaw they know of.

phrases.japanese: 修理したことはありますか？
phrases.romaji: Shūri shita koto wa arimasu ka?
phrases.usageNote: Critical for watches and cameras. Undisclosed repairs can affect resale value and function. Reputable chain shops like Hard Off are usually honest about known service history.
Appropriate for luxury goods, branded clothing, or anything where fakes circulate. JP recycle shops verify authenticity before accepting items — asking confirms you know your market.

phrases.japanese: どこから来た商品ですか？
phrases.romaji: Doko kara kita shōhin desu ka?
phrases.meaning: Where did this item come from?
phrases.usageNote: Asks about provenance. At Hard Off, items come from local seller drop-offs — staff may know if it came from a collector or an estate sale, which can matter for rare pieces.

phrases.japanese: もう少し安くなりますか？
phrases.meaning: Can you make it a little cheaper?
phrases.usageNote: Polite opener that works about 40% of the time. Most effective on items above ¥10,000 or with a yellow sale sticker — those are already marked down and staff have pricing flexibility.

phrases.japanese: まとめて買うので、少し負けてもらえますか？
phrases.romaji: Matomete kau node, sukoshi makete moraemasu ka?
phrases.meaning: I'm buying several — can you give me a small discount?
phrases.usageNote: Most effective phrase when buying 2+ items. Show the pile before asking. Works better at independent shops than chain stores — BookOff and Hard Off staff have limited discount authority.

phrases.japanese: できるだけ安くしてもらえますか？
phrases.romaji: Dekiru dake yasuku shite moraemasu ka?
phrases.meaning: What's the best price you can offer?
phrases.usageNote: More direct than the polite opener. Use when you're serious and want to open a real negotiation. Pair with a pause after asking — silence often prompts a counteroffer.
Stronger than just 動きますか — ちゃんと signals you care about full function, not just power-on. Critical for electronics and cameras in the B/C grade section at Hard Off.
Most shops accommodate this. For cameras, staff often have a battery ready. For audio gear, ask to plug in. Note: Hard Off Junk section items are always sold as-is — skip this there.
Ask before committing to expensive items. Hard Off and BookOff chains generally allow returns within a week for faulty goods. Independent shops often don't — always confirm.
Use after selecting multiple items. Often triggers a spontaneous discount without needing to negotiate — especially when buying 5+ pieces. Show the pile clearly before asking.

phrases.japanese: この３つまとめていくらですか？
phrases.romaji: Kono mittsu matomete ikura desu ka?
phrases.meaning: How much for these three as a bundle?
phrases.usageNote: Specific and polite — more effective than a vague all-in offer. Swap the number as needed: futatsu (2), mittsu (3), yottsu (4), itsutsu (5).

phrases.japanese: 値段がついていないのですが…
phrases.romaji: Nedan ga tsuite inai no desu ga...
phrases.meaning: This doesn't seem to have a price tag...
phrases.usageNote: The trailing ellipsis is intentional — pause after saying it. Common with items in display cases or freshly shelved stock. Staff will either price it on the spot or check with a manager.
Polite form — the お (o-) prefix adds respect. Use when approaching senior staff or before starting a negotiation. Point clearly at what you're asking about.
Slightly more formal than ください — signals you're a respectful buyer. Good habit in higher-end shops or after the seller has been particularly helpful during a test or negotiation.
Most Hard Off and 2nd Street chains accept cards. Smaller independent shops are often cash only. Always carry ¥10,000–20,000 in cash as backup when hitting multiple shops.

phrases.japanese: 領収書をいただけますか？
phrases.usageNote: Essential for customs declarations when taking items home. Keep every receipt — especially for items above your home country's duty-free threshold.

phrases.japanese: 袋に入れてもらえますか？
phrases.meaning: Could you bag this for me?
phrases.usageNote: Japan introduced a plastic bag charge in 2020 — staff may not offer one automatically. Ask if you need it, especially for fragile or bulky items you're taking on the train.

phrases.japanese: 見ているだけです、ありがとう。
phrases.usageNote: Use when approached by staff and not ready to commit. Japanese staff will respect this immediately and give you space — no need to explain further.
Graceful way to walk away without offending. Sometimes prompts a last-minute counteroffer or a mention of a cheaper similar item. Useful when the price isn't quite right.
Definitive but polite decline after inspecting. Less ambiguous than 考えてみます when you've found a dealbreaker. Use after a test or close inspection reveals a problem.
Regular visitors get better treatment over time — staff remember faces. If you find a shop with great stock, say this and mean it. Builds rapport for better negotiation on future visits.
